passages.title: Build from smaller disjoint pieces
passages.text:
A finite rooted tree T is nonempty. Choose one distinguished root r; partition every other node into disjoint nonempty sets T₁,…,Tₖ, each itself a rooted tree. The children of r are their roots. The construction terminates because every child tree has fewer nodes. An ordered tree additionally remembers the list order of these child trees. A forest is an ordered list of zero or more such trees.

Read the symbol ⊔ as “disjoint union”: put these node sets together without sharing a node. The braces {r} mean the set containing only the root. T₁ through Tₖ are the child trees, with k naming how many child trees there are.

passages.title: Names belong to a chosen root
passages.text:
The degree of a node is its number of children, not its total undirected degree. A leaf has degree zero. Set the root level to zero; each parent-to-child step adds one. The subtree rooted at v contains v and all its descendants. Subtrees rooted at different children are disjoint, but the subtree at a parent contains those at its children. This distinction prevents a mistaken claim that all subtrees are disjoint.

The letter ℓ names a level number. Thus ℓ(child)=ℓ(parent)+1 says that following one child edge increases the number of steps from the root by one.

passages.title: Two slots are extra information
passages.text:
A binary tree is either empty, or a root together with a left binary tree and a right binary tree. Its two slots have names. A root with just a left child and a root with just a right child are different binary shapes, even though both have one child. An ordinary one-child ordered tree has no empty first slot to distinguish those cases. Therefore “at most two children” is insufficient as a definition of a binary tree.

In (r,L,R), r is the root node, L the left child tree, and R the right child tree. The symbol ∅ means an empty tree. The order of L and R matters even when one is empty.

passages.title: Why the recursive definition is safe
passages.text:
Prove statements about all finite trees by node-count induction: establish the one-node case, assume the claim for each strictly smaller child tree, and combine them at the root. Unique parenthood follows because the child sets form a partition at every step. Sharing one physical child between two parents violates that partition, even if a drawing looks tree-like. The animation is one instance of this definition, not an induction proof for all sizes.

The bars in |T| mean “number of nodes in tree T”. The 1 counts the root. The sum adds |T₁|, then |T₂|, and so on through |Tₖ|: the node counts of all k child trees. Disjoint child trees ensure that no node is counted twice.

sections.title: Build the idea, then justify it

passages.title: Parentheses describe nesting
passages.text: A recursively nested list consists of atoms and sublists in a specified order. In (a,(b,c),d), the inner list is one element of the outer list; b and c are not siblings of a. An atom is treated as indivisible at this level. Empty sublists are legitimate objects, distinct from a missing pointer. Finite nesting can be expanded into a tree of occurrences, but an implementation need not allocate a fresh object for every occurrence.

passages.title: Equal contents versus one object
passages.text: Let two references lead to the same inner object Q. Reading either reference observes Q; changing Q once is observed through both. Two separately allocated objects with equal contents do not have this property. A shared acyclic structure is a directed acyclic graph of identities, while its expanded occurrence tree may duplicate whole substructures and be much larger. Counting references and counting distinct allocated objects answer different questions.

passages.title: A finite graph can have infinite expansion
passages.text: A reference from a descendant back to an ancestor creates a cycle. The allocated graph may still have only three objects, but recursively printing all descendants without a stopping rule does not terminate. Use an active-ancestor set to detect back-edges while expanding: enter marks an object active; return removes it. Encountering an active identity reports a cycle. A separate completed/visited set avoids revisiting shared objects when the task is to count each identity once.

passages.title: Which promise makes recursion valid?
passages.text: Finite trees justify structural recursion directly because every recursive argument is a smaller subtree. On arbitrary lists-with-sharing, the implementation must specify whether it visits occurrences or distinct identities; on cyclic graphs it must additionally specify a termination policy. A visited set intentionally changes occurrence semantics. Two references to an already completed node indicate sharing, not necessarily a cycle. The box example establishes the difference concretely, not a universal garbage-collection algorithm.

title: Preorder inorder and postorder are timed visits

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition

sections.title: Build the idea, then justify it

passages.title: Arrival is not necessarily a visit
passages.text: A traversal is a control walk through the tree plus a rule for when to emit a node. For a nonempty binary node v, there are three meaningful moments: before the left subtree, between left and right, and after the right subtree. Preorder, inorder and postorder emit at those moments respectively. Returning to a node is not an accidental duplicate visit: it is the moment needed to decide which child work has finished.

passages.title: Exactly once is a theorem
passages.text: Induct on node count. The empty case emits nothing. For a nonempty tree, the induction hypothesis says each child emits all and only its own nodes once. The computed ribbons verify our implementation on this input; they do not replace the induction.

sections.title: Build the idea, then justify it

passages.title: Replace suspended calls with cards
passages.text: An inorder call first asks its left child to finish. Before following that child, save the current node on a last-in-first-out stack S. When the current pointer P is null, the top card identifies the next pending node: pop it, visit it, then set P to its right child. Continue while either P is nonnull or S is nonempty. The frames distinguish pushing, popping, visiting and resuming; popping alone does not emit anything.

passages.title: What a pending ancestor actually means
passages.text: At the descent test, every stack entry is an ancestor whose own visit and right-subtree work have not yet occurred. The top entry is the nearest such ancestor. P names the next subtree to traverse, or null when that subtree is complete. Previously emitted nodes form an initial segment of the desired inorder word. During the pop/visit microsteps, P temporarily names a node rather than an unvisited subtree; the control label is therefore part of the state.

passages.title: Linear work does not imply constant storage
passages.text: Each of n nodes is pushed, popped and visited exactly once. Child tests and pointer updates add only constant work per node, so total time is O(n). The stack contains at most h nodes where h is the number of nodes on a longest root-to-leaf path; auxiliary space is O(h). A balanced tree may have logarithmic height, but a chain has h=n. For the empty tree there are no pushes and no visits.

passages.title: State the header convention, including empty

passages.title: No explicit stack is not the same as one-step queries
passages.text: A successor operation may descend a long left chain, so its worst-case time is O(h). Right-only threading is another valid tradeoff; then empty left children remain null and the successor descent tests for null instead of LTAG.

passages.title: Decode by following sibling chains
passages.text: An empty forest maps to the empty binary tree. For a nonempty forest with first tree (v,C) and remaining forest S, its encoding is (v,encode(C),encode(S)). Conversely, the left subtree decodes to v’s child forest and the right subtree decodes to the remaining roots. Structural induction on node count proves these operations are inverses. This is a bijection between ordered forests and binary trees, not between one rooted tree and every binary tree.

passages.text: Forest preorder emits a root, then its child forest, then its remaining sibling forest: precisely binary preorder. passages.title: Syntax is part of the data structure
passages.text: An expression tree has one operator or operand at every node. Constants and variables have arity zero; unary negation and logarithm have arity one; addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and exponentiation have arity two here. Arity is a property of the operator, not a guess from nearby symbols. Unary negation and binary subtraction must be represented by different operation tags even when both print a minus sign.

passages.title: Prefix and postfix need operator signatures
passages.text: Preorder lists an operator before its operands, producing prefix notation. Postorder lists it after its operands, producing postfix notation. A label sequence alone is insufficient when arities are unspecified: “−” could consume one item or two. The executable evaluator validates arity and rejects missing operands or extra roots.

passages.title: The top of the stack is the rightmost child
passages.text: Scan postfix from left to right. Push an operand’s value. At a d-ary operator, remove the top d values as a group in their existing bottom-to-top order, evaluate the operator on that ordered group, and push the result. For binary subtraction, pop the right operand b, then the left a, and compute a−b. Reversing that order is invisible for addition and multiplication, which makes subtraction and division essential tests.

passages.title: Differentiate structure, not printed characters
passages.text:
Traverse the source expression in postorder. A leaf yields derivative 1 if it is the selected variable x, otherwise 0; every other variable is held constant. At each operator, combine the already-computed child derivatives with the original child expressions. The result is a new immutable AST. Source occurrences remain unchanged, and reused immutable subexpressions are safe; a mutable pointer implementation would need copies or an explicit sharing policy.

AST means abstract syntax tree: a tree whose nodes record the operators and operands of an expression. D means “take the derivative with respect to x”. It creates a new expression describing the rate of change; it does not evaluate the original expression at a chosen number.

passages.title: Why two product terms and an inside factor appear
passages.text:
For differentiable u and v, subtract u(x)v(x) from u(x+h)v(x+h), then add and subtract u(x+h)v(x). Divide by h. The two resulting difference quotients converge to u′v and uv′ because differentiability implies continuity. This proves the product rule. For a composite g(u(x)), the chain rule multiplies g′(u(x)) by u′(x); when the inner increment vanishes, the derivative definition supplies the same limit. Thus x(x+2)² differentiates to (x+2)²+x·2(x+2), including both sources of change.

Read Du and u′ as the derivative of u with respect to x. In g′, the prime means the derivative of g with respect to its own input. The circle ∘ means composition: (g∘u)(x)=g(u(x)), so u runs first and g uses its result. Multiplication by Du supplies the rate at which that inner input changes.

passages.title: Carry conditions with local rewrite rules
passages.text: Addition, subtraction and negation act on derivatives componentwise. D(ln u)=Du/u for u>0. The quotient rule is ((Du)v−u(Dv))/v² for v≠0. For a fixed integer n, D(uⁿ)=n·uⁿ⁻¹Du wherever the power is defined and differentiable, with the zero-exponent constant handled separately. For variable real exponent v, D(uᵛ)=uᵛ[(Dv)ln u+v(Du)/u] on u>0; this follows by writing uᵛ=exp(v ln u) and applying product and chain rules. We do not extend that logarithmic formula blindly to negative bases.

passages.title: Two ways to choose the next family
passages.text: Family order first lists forest roots. Then list the children of the most recently listed node whose family is not yet processed: pending families form a stack. Equivalently it is reverse binary postorder under the first-child/next-sibling encoding. Level order instead processes pending families in FIFO order, so all depth-k nodes precede depth-(k+1) nodes. A queue is essential; replacing it with a stack produces family order, not breadth-first order.

passages.title: Postorder with degrees reconstructs child groups
passages.text: For each postorder record (v,d), pop the top d already-completed trees as an ordered group, make them v’s children, and push that tree. Degree zero consumes nothing. The sequence is invalid if d is negative or exceeds the stack size; duplicate IDs are invalid in this identity-preserving model. At the end, remaining trees are forest roots. A single-tree encoding must leave exactly one; a valid forest may leave several. This is a different representation-specific sufficiency claim from preorder tag redundancy.

passages.title: The proof restores the older stack prefix
passages.text: Fix an arbitrary stack prefix before a subtree’s postorder block. For a leaf, push its value and leave the prefix untouched. By induction, each child block adds exactly its child result above that prefix, in family order. The parent step consumes those d results and replaces them by f(v). Therefore the whole block adds exactly one result without disturbing older completed trees. Repeating this across a forest leaves one result per root.

passages.title: Separate traversal cost from local computation
passages.text: The structural stack work is linear in the number of nodes because each result is pushed once and popped at most once. Total computation also includes the costs of the local functions; symbolic expressions can grow large, so linear visits do not imply linear output size. A star can leave many child results on the stack even though its height is small. Unlike the ancestor stack for binary inorder, this value stack is not automatically bounded by tree height.

passages.title: An update must restore every advertised relation
passages.text: If a node is inserted between siblings a and b in a doubly linked family, update a.next, new.prev, new.next and b.prev, as well as the new node’s parent. Circular/ring conventions replace null family ends by specified return links; the sentinel policy must be stated before traversal. More links usually simplify some navigation while increasing update obligations and storage.

passages.title: Parent-only trees are useful for equivalence classes
passages.text: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and partitions a set into disjoint classes. Start with each element as its own root. To process a pair a≡b, follow parent links to both roots and, if they differ, attach one root to the other. Representatives agree exactly when the processed relations imply membership in the same class. Our model uses root.parent=root, unlike the source’s null-root sentinel; neither convention changes the partition.

passages.title: The trie is algebra, the ring is an implementation
passages.text: The source stores UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT links, together with exponent EXP and coefficient-or-variable CV. This demonstration actually mutates a bounded instance: insert a fresh coefficient into the circular sibling ring, cancel and unlink it, collapse a constant-only coefficient, then collapse the root from y to x. The surviving x children retain their identities, but their UP links must be changed to the surviving root address. Each committed operation is checked against an independent exponent dictionary; noncanonical intermediate headers are explicitly marked. This executes the insertion, unlink and collapse mechanics, not every branch of general Algorithm A. Tree storage is not always smaller or faster than a sparse list; workload and coefficient costs determine that tradeoff.

passages.title: Connected and acyclic means one simple route
passages.text: Connectedness supplies a path between any two distinct vertices. If two different simple paths joined the same pair, take their first divergence and their next reunion; the two intervening portions form a cycle. Therefore an acyclic connected graph has exactly one simple path between each pair. Conversely a cycle supplies two different simple routes between vertices on that cycle, contradicting uniqueness. This proves the characterization; the finite animation only illustrates it.

passages.title: Why n−1 edges follows, and what it does not say alone
passages.text: Every finite acyclic graph with at least one edge has a leaf: an endpoint of a longest simple path cannot have another neighbor without extending the path or making a cycle. Remove a leaf and its one edge; repeat by induction. A forest with n vertices and c components has m=n−c edges. Thus a connected forest has n−1 edges. Conversely, a connected graph contains a spanning tree with n−1 edges; if it already has exactly that many, no additional cycle edge remains.

passages.title: Every tree edge is indispensable
passages.text: Removing an edge uv of a tree disconnects u from v, because any remaining path would combine with uv into a cycle. Conversely, if a connected graph loses connectedness whenever any edge is deleted, it cannot contain a cycle: removing one cycle edge would leave an alternative route. A one-vertex graph with no edges satisfies the tree characterizations vacuously. The numerical equalities require finite graphs; do not subtract infinite cardinalities as though this proof applied.

sections.title: Build the idea, then justify it

passages.title: A spanning tree chooses independent cycle coordinates
passages.text: For this flow model, forget arc directions but retain distinct edge identities: opposite or parallel arcs become parallel undirected edges rather than being merged. In that connected underlying multigraph with n vertices and m edge occurrences, choose a spanning tree. Each of the m−n+1 non-tree edges closes a unique cycle with the tree path joining its endpoints; a loop, if present, is a one-edge cycle. Assign an arbitrary reference direction to each edge, and record +1 for traversing with it, −1 against it, 0 otherwise. These signed fundamental-cycle vectors are algebraic objects; they need not be directed executable cycles.

passages.title: Conservation is a linear equation
passages.text:
Let B have one column per directed edge: +1 at its tail, −1 at its head, zero elsewhere. For a loop these contributions cancel in the same row. For an edge-count vector f, Bf is outgoing count minus incoming count at each vertex. A start-to-stop walk has Bf=1_s−1_t; if s=t, this is zero. A fixed signed spanning-tree path p has the same divergence. Thus f−p is a circulation in the nullspace of B.

B is the incidence matrix: each column records where one directed edge leaves and arrives. The bold symbol 1_s is a vector with 1 in the row for the start vertex s and 0 in every other row; 1_t does the same for the stop vertex. The vector c_j records the signed edge counts of fundamental cycle j. Consequently Bc_j=0 says that this cycle has no net surplus departure at any vertex.

passages.title: Why the fundamental cycles span uniquely
passages.text:
Each fundamental cycle contains its own non-tree edge with coefficient +1 and no other non-tree edge. Subtract from a circulation the matching multiple of every such cycle. The remainder is supported only on tree edges. At a leaf, zero divergence forces its sole remaining edge coefficient to be zero; deleting leaves repeatedly makes every coefficient zero. This proves spanning. The unique non-tree coordinates prove independence, hence cycle-space dimension m−n+1 for a connected graph.

In the formula, f is the complete edge-count vector and p is a chosen start-to-stop path vector. The index j names a fundamental cycle; c_j is that cycle’s signed edge-count vector, and α_j tells how many signed copies to add. The summation adds these contributions for all m−n+1 non-tree edges. This is a vector equation: it must hold separately for every edge.

passages.title: Linear solutions are not automatically executions
passages.text: For a realizable directed walk, each final edge count must be a nonnegative integer, with the specified endpoint imbalance, and all vertices touching positive-count edges must lie in one weakly connected component containing the endpoints when the walk is nonempty. These conditions are also sufficient: replace an edge with f_e distinct parallel tickets and apply the directed Euler-trail theorem. They describe possible walks in the flow graph, not whether a particular program’s data-dependent branch tests will actually choose that walk.

passages.title: The source points parent arcs toward the root
passages.text: The book’s oriented tree is a rooted-unordered tree drawn as a digraph with arcs from children toward parents. Every nonroot has outdegree one, the root has outdegree zero, and every vertex can reach the root. In modern terminology this is an inward arborescence. An outward arborescence reverses all arrows: root indegree zero, every other indegree one, and the root reaches every vertex. State which convention is being used before applying a degree test.

passages.title: Degree constraints need a global condition
passages.text: Choose a root R in a free tree. For each v≠R, direct its first edge on the unique simple path toward R. Degree rules alone are insufficient: a root with no outgoing arc can coexist with a separate directed cycle whose vertices each have outdegree one.

passages.title: Weak connectivity is weaker than reachability
passages.text: A directed graph may have loops and several distinct arcs with the same endpoints. Its underlying simple graph forgets directions, drops loops and merges duplicates. Connectivity of that underlying graph is weak connectivity. Strong connectivity requires directed paths between every pair. The source calls a digraph rooted when some R is reachable from every vertex; this is weaker than strong connectivity and is not the outward “root reaches all” convention. A chain aimed at its final vertex is rooted but not strongly connected.

passages.title: The exact existence conditions
passages.text:
For a closed circuit with at least one arc, every nonisolated vertex has equal indegree and outdegree, and the nonisolated support is weakly connected. For an open trail from s to t, s has outdegree−indegree=1, t has −1, all others have zero, and that support is weakly connected. Necessity follows by pairing every arrival with a departure except at the two endpoints. For the empty arc set, our implementation returns an empty tour; choosing its resting vertex is a separate convention.

Read deg⁺(v) as the number of outgoing arcs at vertex v and deg⁻(v) as the number of incoming arcs. The indicator 1_{v=s} is 1 when v is the start s and 0 otherwise; the indicator for t works the same way. Thus the formula gives +1 at a distinct start, −1 at a distinct stop, and 0 elsewhere. When start and stop coincide, the two indicators cancel.

passages.title: Why taking detours can finish the tour
passages.text: In a balanced finite digraph, following unused outgoing arcs cannot first get stuck away from the starting vertex: arrivals and departures would be unbalanced there. This yields a closed detour. If unused arcs remain, weak connectivity supplies a vertex of the current tour incident with unused support; balance of the remaining arcs supplies an unused departure there. Build another closed detour and splice it in. Repeat until no arc remains. Our stack implementation records return tickets in reverse order, then reverses them. For an open trail, add one temporary t→s arc, construct a circuit, then cut at that arc.

passages.title: Saving the last exit explains the rooted tree
passages.text: In a completed closed tour ending at R, select each nonroot vertex’s last outgoing ticket. If such a ticket leads to another nonroot, that vertex’s last exit occurs strictly later in the tour; otherwise the walk could not leave it and eventually finish at R. Strictly increasing positions rule out a selected cycle. Every nonroot has one selected exit, so all selected paths reach R: an inward spanning tree. Conversely, in a balanced digraph with a chosen inward spanning tree, save each nonroot’s tree exit until its other outgoing tickets are spent. A maximal no-repeated-ticket walk from R then uses every arc. The proof follows any supposed unused ticket along reserved parent exits toward R, contradicting maximality.
